scope: Append-only revalidation of high-priority aggregate candidates. The Faroe lower bound is corrected for documented imported-grain dependence; Fayyum/Nile, Japan, China, Andes and Oceania records remain validation-only because they lack a defensible same-boundary local-food saturation interval or fail the EU5 coverage gate.

promotion_audit.decision: One corrected Faroe one-sided lower bound is admitted. No new two-sided global scale anchor is promoted. All other records remain validation-only with exact missing evidence retained.
promotion_audit.review_method: Reviewed primary or scholarly sources for date, population semantics, local-food dependence, pressure/saturation evidence, shocks and historical boundary. Starting population, HYDE, RGO and modern population fields are excluded.
promotion_audit.reason_faroe_is_one_sided: The 1298 land-management system and stable 3000-4000 population support a local-food floor, but the 2020 metabolic review documents imported grain at about 25 percent of the traditional diet. Therefore an observed 1327 population cannot be treated as an intrinsic local-food upper capacity without an independent food-balance model.
required_followup: Fayyum/Nile: reconstruct a closed village or rural-catchment polygon and obtain a population interval and saturation/pressure evidence independent of fiscal output and Cairo provisioning.
Japan: obtain province-level non-rice fields, household/population intervals and an upper land-scarcity or famine-pressure endpoint; register acreage alone remains a floor.
China: map the six-county Pingjiang Lu boundary and separate local rural food production from canal redistribution, then find a source-supported saturation interval.
Andes: map the raised-field/terrace production footprint and find a date-matched population interval with local pressure; city or basin reconstructions alone are not sufficient.
Tongatapu: repair the 52 percent EU5 area mismatch and resolve the conflict between Green/Burley capacity estimates and later LiDAR population estimates before quantitative use.

records.label: Faroe Islands c.1298-1327: corrected local-support floor under imported-grain uncertainty
records.interval_semantics: The 1327 population endpoints are the two official historical estimates (approximately 2,700 and 4,000); 3,350 is their transparent midpoint for diagnostics. The lower-bound capacity values are population multiplied by a conservative 0.70-0.90 local-food share, not a two-sided natural-capacity ceiling. This supersedes the earlier 0.90 local-food floor because the traditional diet review documents imported grain near 25 percent.

derivation.population_source: Statistics Faroe Islands IB08010, 1327 footnote: approximately 4,000 (Degn) and 2,700 (Guttesen)
derivation.population_interval_rule: Published estimates are retained as low/high; arithmetic midpoint is diagnostic only
derivation.local_food_rule: 0.70 lower bound and 0.75 central follow the documented approximately 25 percent imported-grain share, with 0.90 as an upper sensitivity for geographic/temporal variation
derivation.capacity_rule: One-sided local-support floor equals population endpoint times local-food endpoint; no saturation fraction is inferred
derivation.supersession_rule: Replaces faroe_1300_local_support_floor_wave3 and removes its unsupported 0.90 minimum local-food assumption

pressure_evidence: The 1298 Seyðabrævið (Sheep Letter) codified local pasture and livestock limits: stock should remain at the previous level unless the land can accommodate more, linking land management to an explicit ecological cap.

The Faroese social-metabolism synthesis reports that population rose to roughly 3,000-4,000 and remained stable for five centuries, and that traditional land units were a culturally negotiated carrying-capacity system.
The Norse Faroe rangeland model computes maximum ewe/lamb pairs for geographically representative areas and documents local population pressure, pasture regulation and soil/vegetation constraints.
The historical ecology review finds local resilience from livestock, barley, fish, seabirds and marine mammals, while also reporting that imported grain was an integral staple.
shock_flags: the 1327 population values are retrospective household estimates, not an enumeration
imported grain and maritime exchange are required for part of the traditional diet
pasture caps limit livestock but do not by themselves bound marine or crop calories
severe winters and failed fish/grain years can produce temporary starvation
records.trade_dependence: mixed; traditional local production was substantial but imported grain supplied approximately one quarter of calories in the reviewed balance
records.food_regime: dairy and hay-fed cattle, sheep, barley, swedes, inshore fish, seabirds, pilot whale and seal products with imported grain
records.boundary_description: Complete Faroe archipelago, represented by the EU5 Torshavn location; the declared 0.986 coverage retains unresolved islet/coast clipping.
records.source_family_independence: This is a semantic revalidation of the prior Faroe floor, not an independent source-family replication. It adds the official 1327 estimates and an explicit imported-grain balance; it does not use EU5 starting population.
citation_details: Statistics Faroe Islands IB08010, year 1327 footnote: approximately 4,000 from Anton Degn and approximately 2,700 from Rolf Guttesen.

Social Metabolism of Quiet Sustainability (Sustainability 2020), pp. 6-7: population stable around 3,000-4,000 for five centuries; imported grain close to 25 percent of the traditional diet; one mørk could sustain 40-48 sheep and half a mørk was a minimum family holding.
Sustainable Rangeland Grazing in Norse Faroe, pp. 4-8 and 16-20: 1298 Sheep Letter and modeled local pasture stocking limits/pressure.
Lex Danmarkshistorien: approximately 4,000 around 1300 and economically sustainable until the late eighteenth century; used as qualitative corroboration, not as a narrow capacity endpoint.
records.notes: The corrected one-sided lower bound is the only Faroe quantity admitted to training. It avoids converting a mixed local/imported diet into an intrinsic two-sided capacity target. The old floor is superseded rather than silently retained.

records.label: Fayyum/Nile c.1245: cadastral and population reconstruction recheck
records.interval_semantics: Rapoport's approximately 75,000 Fayyum estimate is retained as a point observation from fiscal reconstruction; no uncertainty interval is invented and it is not a carrying-capacity interval.
pressure_evidence: Al-Nabulusi's 1245 survey records village land, water rights, irrigation and taxes, exposing a local agricultural system but not total population.
Rapoport's reconstruction separates cultivated area, irrigation, subsistence and commercial crops, but the available review does not publish a saturation interval or complete local-calorie share.
Nile irrigation, crop taxation and Cairo/royal transfers make fiscal output an unreliable upper-capacity label without a closed rural boundary.
shock_flags: poll-tax entries cover only non-Muslims
fiscal values are not headcounts or production totals
Madinat al-Fayyum urban population is embedded in the estimate
iqta/endowment and Nile redistribution flows are not separated
records.trade_dependence: mixed; local Nile production is documented but fiscal and urban redistribution are unresolved
records.food_regime: Nile-irrigated wheat, barley, fava beans, rice in suitable pockets, livestock, pasture and fisheries
records.boundary_description: Fayyum depression and surveyed village system; no audited EU5 rural-catchment polygon.
records.source_family_independence: Independent fiscal and scholarly reconstruction sources, but no target is admitted without boundary and saturation closure.
records.notes: Validation-only. Exact missing evidence: same-boundary rural population interval, local-food share, saturation/pressure upper endpoint and EU5 polygon crosswalk.

records.label: Japan provinces c.1280: registered rice-field floors without upper capacity
records.interval_semantics: Farris Great Land Register acreage can establish province-level cultivated-food floors after crop and non-rice sensitivities, but the registers are not complete population counts and do not provide upper saturation endpoints.
pressure_evidence: Farris Tables 1.1-1.3 compare registered rice acreage with estate surveys and document a local cultivated-food base.
Late Heian/Kamakura famine and grain-shortage context supports pressure, but no independent province-specific saturation fraction is resolved.
The register is rice-centered and omits non-rice fields, fisheries and forest foods that are essential to a full Malthusian capacity estimate.
shock_flags: partial registers and omitted non-rice fields
Mongol invasion/provisioning exposure for Kyushu
no province-level upper endpoint or population enumeration
records.trade_dependence: low_to_mixed; local rice and dry fields are documented but regional exchange is not quantified
records.food_regime: wet rice, dry fields, pulses, coastal/river fisheries, livestock and forest foods
records.boundary_description: Multiple historical Japanese provinces; a single EU5 national selector cannot replace province-specific boundary mapping.
records.source_family_independence: Same documentary family as existing Japan lower-bound packets; this recheck prevents rice acreage from being promoted to a two-sided population label.
records.notes: Validation-only. Existing province lower bounds remain the only training use; exact missing evidence is an upper population/saturation endpoint and complete province crosswalk.

records.label: Pingjiang Lu/Suzhou c.1290: dense irrigated register and canal redistribution
records.interval_semantics: Pingjiang Lu's 1290 register gives 466,158 households and 2,433,700 people for six counties. The value is retained as a point administrative observation, not a published uncertainty or carrying-capacity interval.
pressure_evidence: The six-county aggregate is a dense irrigated rice/canal landscape and a useful thriving local-intensive validation case.
Taihu freshwater fisheries, canal transport and administrative redistribution are integral to the system but their imported/local shares are not quantified.
No boundary-matched land-scarcity, real-wage, famine-sensitivity or marginal-land evidence establishes saturation.
shock_flags: Yuan register is administrative and may omit unregistered groups
six-county boundary is not matched to EU5 locations
canal and market redistribution confounds intrinsic local capacity
records.trade_dependence: high; canal and administrative redistribution are central
records.food_regime: irrigated rice, wheat, legumes, pigs, Taihu fisheries and canal markets
records.boundary_description: Pingjiang Lu six counties around Suzhou; not the modern city polygon and not a closed rural-food catchment.
records.source_family_independence: Independent administrative-register source family, but no carrying-capacity label is inferred from the register.
records.notes: Validation-only thriving system. Exact missing evidence: mappable six-county crosswalk, local-food share and an independent saturation interval that excludes canal redistribution.

records.label: Lake Titicaca raised-field basin c.1000-1400: local intensification without a boundary-matched capacity target
records.interval_semantics: Raised-field and frost-mitigation archaeology establishes feasible local intensification, but the reviewed basin studies do not provide a single date-matched rural population interval and saturation fraction for a closed EU5 boundary.
pressure_evidence: Archaeological syntheses document raised fields, frost-risk management, wetland agriculture and dense settlement in the Lake Titicaca basin.
The basin includes Tiwanaku and later regional polities with labor mobilization and exchange; city/ritual centers cannot supervise surrounding land capacity.
No independent local-food pressure series resolves whether the 1000-1400 footprint was at equilibrium or below its technical potential.
shock_flags: broad basin boundary spans multiple ecological zones
Tiwanaku political collapse and later Inca expansion alter land use
population estimates are archaeological extrapolations with no saturation interval
records.trade_dependence: mixed; local tubers, quinoa, raised-field crops and camelids with regional exchange
records.food_regime: raised-field potatoes/tubers, quinoa, chenopods, camelids, fish and wetland foods
records.boundary_description: Lake Titicaca basin raised-field and wetland agricultural complexes; no closed historical rural polygon reconstructed.
records.source_family_independence: Independent Andean archaeology and agronomy sources; no population label is inferred.
records.notes: Validation-only physical case. Exact missing evidence: one mappable rural aggregate, date-matched population interval and independent saturation/pressure endpoint.

records.label: Tongatapu c.1100-1500: explicit capacity envelope but unresolved area and chronology
records.interval_semantics: Green/Kirch/Burley reconstruct an explicit 18,000-24,000 agricultural capacity envelope and late-prehistoric population estimates, but the chronology, source-family dependence and EU5 area mismatch prevent training use.
pressure_evidence: Green's reconstruction uses 1.8-2.0 acres per person and an 8-10 year bush-fallow cycle, with pressure/reduction mechanisms beginning around 60-80 percent of capacity.
Archaeobotanical work documents near-complete primary-forest removal, intensive multi-cropping, fallow pressure and political expansion after local intensification limits.
The later LiDAR/Bayesian estimate of 50,000-60,000 is a different chronology/quantity and is retained as a conflict diagnostic rather than averaged into the envelope.
shock_flags: warfare and demographic reduction mechanisms
deforestation and fallow pressure
chiefdom tribute/inter-island expansion
EU5 calibrated footprint is approximately 52 percent of the cited island area in the closure audit
Green/Kirch/Burley capacity family is shared and model-derived
records.food_regime: yam, taro, sweet potato, banana, breadfruit, coconut, pigs, fisheries and local horticulture
records.boundary_description: Entire Tongatapu island; historical arable area is approximately 224 km2 and the EU5 selector is location_tag=tongatapu.
records.source_family_independence: Same shared capacity family as the existing Tongatapu validation packet; this recheck is not independent replication.
records.notes: Validation-only. Repair the area crosswalk and resolve the LiDAR chronology/quantity conflict before any quantitative scoring; do not silently rescale the 52 percent footprint.
